questions.key_step: Moving the bracket terms together makes both sides factorise with the common factor (x-1).
questions.justification: Factor out (x-1) after collecting bracket terms, then rule out {x}=3; short and familiar.

questions.key_step: The functional equation forces f(k)=3^k, so the sum is a geometric series.
questions.justification: One familiar idea: f(k)=3^k, then a GP sum.

questions.key_step: Show f(x)+f(1-x)=1 and pair the terms equidistant from the two ends of the sum.
questions.justification: Pairing f(x)+f(1-x)=1 is a standard trick; routine verification.

questions.key_step: Range [0,2] means the argument takes exactly the values [1,m], and sqrt2(sin x-cos x) ranges over [-2,2].
questions.justification: Range of a sin-cos expression plus log range matching; two routine steps.

questions.key_step: Subtracting the two conditions removes lambda and leaves 5^n-4^n=61.
questions.justification: Subtract to eliminate lambda, find n by inspection, divisor sum.

questions.key_step: Everything is determined by f(1); the bound |f(4)|le8 leaves only two integer values of f(1).
questions.justification: Eliminate to f(4)=3-6f(1), bound, two cases; a few routine steps.

questions.key_step: List every restriction: argument, base, the inner log_e x, and a non-zero denominator.
questions.justification: Four standard domain conditions listed and intersected.

questions.key_step: Subtract the relation for n from that for n+1 to get (n+1)f(n+1)=nf(n), so nf(n) is constant.
questions.justification: Subtract consecutive sum relations to get nf(n) constant; one standard move then arithmetic.

questions.key_step: The domain is [-2,3]; f increases then decreases with the maximum at x=frac12.
questions.justification: Domain, derivative zero, three evaluations; routine multi-step.

questions.key_step: On each interval [n,n+1), [x]=n is constant and dfrac n{1+x^2} decreases, so every piece is a half-open interval.
questions.justification: Piecewise range on four unit intervals with overlap check; routine but careful.

questions.key_step: x^2-x+1 is always positive, so f=g+[g] with g minimal at the vertex x=frac12.
questions.justification: Note the quadratic is positive and min at the vertex; floor part monotone.

questions.key_step: Substituting x=2, frac12, -1 cycles through the same three points and gives three linear equations.
questions.justification: Three substitutions in the cycle x -> 1/(1-x); standard functional-equation trick.

questions.key_step: f(1)subsetneq f(2)subsetneqcdotssubsetneq f(6) is a chain of six sets with six different sizes out of 0,1,dots,6: exactly one size is skipped.
questions.justification: Counting strict chains of subsets with six distinct sizes; seven size patterns with many slips possible, no options to check.
questions.nearest_anchor: 2023-P1-Q1 (L4, functions on small sets); precision risk (F2)

questions.key_step: Invert the given inverse to get (fcirc g)(x)=2x^3+7 and compare with a(x^b+c)-3.
questions.justification: Invert the given inverse, match coefficients, two evaluations; routine.

questions.key_step: The additive equation with f(1)=frac15 gives f(n)=frac n5, and the sum then telescopes.
questions.justification: f(n)=n/5 then standard telescoping.

questions.key_step: Compose step by step; the coefficients follow the pattern (3x+2),(13x+12),(63x+62),(313x+312),(1563x+1562).
questions.justification: Repeated composition of a Mobius map; careful arithmetic over five steps.

questions.key_step: Find which products mcdot n stay inside A; apart from the trivial ones with 1, only 3cdot3=9 gives a real condition.
questions.justification: Spot that only 3x3=9 gives a condition; short counting.

questions.key_step: [x+k]=[x]+k simplifies A to [x]le-2; the geometric series equals frac13, which simplifies B to 27<3^{-3x}.
questions.justification: Two routine simplifications (floor shift and GP) and a set comparison.

questions.key_step: [x]-x is zero exactly on integers and lies in (0,1) otherwise, so f>1 on mathbb R-mathbb Z.
questions.justification: Ceiling function domain and range, then two set statements.

questions.key_step: f has the form frac{Ax+B}{Cx-A} (trace zero), so f(f(x))=x and the sum is x+frac4x.
questions.justification: f(f(x))=x by direct substitution, then AM-GM.

questions.key_step: Solve the quadratic inequality for the integer [x], then convert back to x.
questions.justification: Quadratic inequality in [x] and conversion back to x; one familiar move.

questions.key_step: Write x+3-sqrt x in terms of g=sqrt x+1 to get f(t)=t^2-3t+5 - but only on the range tge1 of g.
questions.justification: Rewrite fog in terms of g; the catch is the range of g (Bonus question).

questions.key_step: Count all onto functions, then subtract those with f(a)=1, splitting by whether the other four elements also hit 1.
questions.justification: Two counting steps for onto functions with a restriction.

questions.key_step: For the first equation use [x]>x-1 to show the left side is positive away from [5,6); the second splits at x=-2.
questions.justification: Two separate root counts: floor-quadratic needs a careful argument, modulus equation is casework.

questions.key_step: f(4)=f(1)+f(2)+1le6 forces f(1)+f(2)le5; f(3) and f(5) are free.
questions.justification: Condition fixes f(4); casework on the sum of two values.

questions.key_step: [sqrt k]=r for r^2le k<(r+1)^2, so the value r occurs 2r+1 times.
questions.justification: Group values of floor(sqrt k) and sum an arithmetic-quadratic series.

questions.key_step: Sum f in closed form by the S-xS trick, then evaluate 2f(2)+f'(2).
questions.justification: Closed form of an arithmetico-geometric sum and evaluation of f(2), f'(2) with large numbers.

questions.key_step: Different numbers can share the same largest prime factor, and the range contains only primes.
questions.justification: Two counterexamples for one-one and onto.

questions.key_step: Domain of fcirc g = {xintext{dom }g: g(x)intext{dom }f}: exclude x=-frac52 and any x with g(x)=-frac12.
questions.justification: Composition domain: second condition needs a short check of g(x)=-1/2.

questions.key_step: The values of g all lie in [0,3], where f(t)=1-frac t3; then read the range off each piece.
questions.justification: Evaluate the composite on pieces; identify the unused branch.

questions.key_step: The domain is the intersection of frac{2x+3}{4x^2+x-3}>0 and -1lefrac{2x-1}{x+2}le1; each is a sign-chart problem.
questions.justification: Two sign-chart inequalities and an intersection; long but routine.

questions.key_step: fcirc f simplifies to the identity, so any number of compositions of g returns the input.
questions.justification: f o f simplifies to identity: one trick.

questions.key_step: Work out g(f(x)) piece by piece (the sign of f(x) decides the branch of g), then read off the graph.
questions.justification: Piecewise composition with the sign of f deciding g's branch; then one-one/onto tests.

questions.key_step: Intersect x^2-25ge0, x^2ne4 and x^2+2x-15>0; the first two are met automatically for |x|ge5.
questions.justification: Intersect three standard domain conditions.

questions.key_step: Each f(a) is a subset of A containing a: the other 6 elements are free, giving 2^6 choices per element.
questions.justification: Each f(a) is a subset containing a: 2^6 per element; one counting idea.

questions.key_step: List the ordered pairs of distinct elements of B with sum 14, then map the remaining three elements one-one into the remaining five.
questions.justification: Ordered pairs with sum 14 then injective assignment of the rest.

questions.key_step: Compute f(g(x)) on xge0 and x<0 and look at the graph: it is symmetric-looking with a vertex at the origin and range [0,infty).
questions.justification: Composition of piecewise functions, then graph reading.

questions.key_step: A derivative that changes sign shows f is many-one; the range is a bounded interval, so f is not onto mathbb R.
questions.justification: Derivative sign change shows many-one; onto needs the range; two standard checks.

questions.key_step: -1lesin5xle1 gives 6le7-sin5xle8 and reciprocals reverse the inequality.
questions.justification: Bounds on sin and reciprocal; one familiar step.

questions.key_step: Evaluate f at the five primes; if the five values are distinct the range has 5 elements and the count is 5!.
questions.justification: Evaluate floor-log at five primes and count injections; careful arithmetic.

questions.key_step: For x>0 both f(|x|) and |f(x)| equal x+a, so g=0 on (0,a]; for x<0, g=-frac x2lefrac a2.
questions.justification: Piecewise g with modulus and f(|x|); isolated point x=0 is a trap; then one-one/onto.

questions.key_step: Compute a=109 and b=2, then use e^2=1-frac ba and l=frac{2b}{sqrt a} for the ellipse frac{x^2}{a}+frac{y^2}{b}=1.
questions.justification: Two compositions then ellipse formulas; routine chain.

questions.key_step: sin3x+cos3xin[-sqrt2,sqrt2] gives the extremes of f; then compute the two means.
questions.justification: Range of sin+cos then AM and GM; single standard idea.

questions.justification: Iterate f, spot the pattern 1,5,21,85 and generalise to the 10th term.

questions.key_step: Split on the sign of 2a-1 and use a=[a]+{a} to turn each case into an equation for the integer part.
questions.justification: Casework on |2a-1| with integer and fractional parts; careful bounds on [a].

questions.key_step: f(n)=n on mathbb N, so the sum is an arithmetic series in lambda.
questions.justification: f(n)=n then arithmetic-series inequality.

questions.key_step: List the natural solutions of 2x+3y=23; A and B both have 4 elements, so one-one means a bijection.
questions.justification: List solutions of a linear equation and count bijections.
